newsitem.title: USA: GM sees international profit pressure.
newsitem.headline: GM sees international profit pressure.

text.p: General Motors Corp signalled that 1997 profits from its international operations may be flat with or below the $1.53 billion they earned in 1996, analysts said Monday.

J.P. Morgan analyst David Bradley said GM executives told analysts in a conference call that Europe's slumping car market and heavy expenses for for new plants in Poland, Argentina, Thailand and China will hurt the International Operations' profitability in 1997.
"They've given us some guidance that international earnings are going to be under pressure in 1997," Bradley said. "I don't think the expectation is that they'll go up."

Prudential Securities analyst Philip Fricke said GM executives also expect higher foreign tax rates in 1997 than in 1996, which would lead to a reduction in net earnings even if operating earnings were flat.
The $1.53 billion in 1996 international earnings represents a 6.7 percent decline from the $1.64 billion the operations earned in 1994.

In the fourth quarter of 1996, GM's European automotive operations earned only $99 million in the fourth quarter, down from $248 million a year earlier. For the full 1996 year, GM-Europe earned $778 million, down from $796 million in 1995.
"Europe will continue to be tough in 1997," GM Chief Financial Officer J. Michael Losh told reporters in a separate conference call.
In a statement accompanying the automaker's fourth quarter 1996 earnings results, GM Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Jack Smith said the international plant building binge will pay dividends.

"We have embarked on the largest international production-capacity expansion in our history with major new manufacturing and assembly facilitiies planned for key international regions," Smith said. "Those facilities will provide us with significant opportuities to leverage GM's global resources and enhance our competitive position throughout the world."
